opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest starting point is admitting that we mostly don't measure this at all right now. The evaluations that get the most attention are capability benchmarks: can the model pass the bar exam, solve the math problem, write the code. Those tell you what the system can do. They tell you almost nothing about what happens to the person using it over weeks and months.

So the first thing it will take is a shift in the unit of analysis. Instead of asking "did the model produce a good answer," we have to ask "is the person better or worse off at the end of this interaction, and at the end of a semester, and at the end of a year?" That's a fundamentally different kind of study. It's longitudinal, it's messy, and it looks a lot more like education research or public health than like a leaderboard.

Second, we need to get clear on what we're actually trying to protect. Learning isn't just getting the right answer. A lot of it happens in the struggle: the productive confusion, retrieving something you half-remember, building a mental model that you can carry into a new situation. A system that removes all friction can feel incredibly helpful in the moment while quietly hollowing out the skill. So evaluations need to look at things like transfer, retention, and whether someone can do the task *without* the tool afterward, not just whether they finished it faster with it.

Third, there's the incentive problem, which I think is the heart of it. If the companies building these systems are measured on engagement and daily active use, then a product that makes you dependent on it looks like a success on the dashboard. We've seen this movie before with social media. So independent evaluation matters a lot: researchers, educators, maybe public institutions with real access to these systems and the data, not just voluntary disclosures on the companies' terms.

And finally, I'd say we need to include the people most affected in designing the evaluations. Teachers, students, parents, people learning new jobs. They notice things that a lab metric won't catch, like a kid who stops trusting their own judgment, or a junior employee who never develops intuition because the answer was always handed to them.

None of this is impossible. We know how to run careful studies on learning. What's been missing is the will to treat cognitive effects as a first-class safety question rather than an afterthought. If we can make that shift now, while these tools are still being woven into classrooms and workplaces, we have a real chance to build AI that makes people more capable rather than less.

r001.rationale: The response calls for longitudinal studies of human outcomes and names learning measures such as transfer and retention, but it does not state that real-world human-subjects research is needed to determine which AI model behaviors to track.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that we don't yet have the evaluation infrastructure to answer that question well, and the first step is admitting that.

Right now, almost all of our AI evaluation is about the model. Is it accurate, is it helpful, does it refuse the right things, how does it score on a benchmark. What we almost never measure is the person on the other side of the screen six months later. Did they get better at the thing they were using the tool for, or did they get worse at it while feeling like they got better? That gap, between perceived competence and actual competence, is the thing I worry about most, and it's invisible in a one-turn evaluation.

So to evaluate effects on cognition and learning, I think you need a few things.

First, you need longitudinal studies, not snapshots. The relevant unit of analysis is not a single interaction, it's a person over weeks or months with and without the tool. We did this for calculators, we did it badly and late for social media, and we should do it on purpose this time, before adoption is total rather than after.

Second, you need to measure retention and transfer, not just task completion. If a student finishes an essay with an AI assistant, that tells you nothing. What you want to know is whether, a month later, they can structure an argument without it. Whether they can notice when the model is wrong. Whether the skill transferred to a context where the tool wasn't there. Those are harder, slower measurements, and they're the ones that actually matter.

Third, you need to look at what I'd call the dependency curve. Every tool offloads some cognition. That's fine, that's what tools are for. The question is whether the offloading is scaffolding, which you eventually take away, or whether it's a substitution that quietly removes the practice people need to build the capacity in the first place. Those look identical on day one. They look very different on day two hundred.

And fourth, and this is the uncomfortable one, the people building these systems have to be willing to measure things that might make their product look worse. A system optimized for engagement and immediate satisfaction will beat one that occasionally makes you struggle, because struggle is unpleasant and it's also where learning happens. If the only metrics are retention and thumbs-up, you will systematically select for tools that feel good and hollow people out. So part of what it takes is institutional, not technical. Independent researchers need access, and there need to be consequences attached to the results.

I'd add one more thing. We should be especially careful about children and about anyone in a formative stage of some skill, because that's where the cost of getting this wrong is highest and least reversible. An expert using AI as a thinking partner is a very different case from a twelve-year-old who has never written a paragraph alone. Our evaluations need to distinguish those, and right now they mostly don't.

r001.rationale: The response calls for longitudinal studies of people using AI and measuring learning outcomes, but it does not state that human-subjects research is needed to determine which AI model behaviors to track.

astra-6.text:
I think we have to start by distinguishing between helping someone complete a task and helping someone learn. Those can look identical in the moment: you get a better essay, you solve the problem faster. But the real question is, what happens when you take the AI away? Does the person understand more? Can they apply what they’ve learned to a different problem? Can they recognize when an answer is wrong?

So we need studies that follow people over time, rather than just measuring performance in a single session. And we need to compare different ways of designing these systems. An AI that immediately supplies an answer may have very different effects from one that asks you to explain your reasoning or gives you a hint.

I’d also want us to look beyond accuracy to things like curiosity, confidence, and the willingness to struggle with something difficult. Some friction is part of learning. The challenge is figuring out which friction gets in the way and which friction helps us develop. That takes collaboration between educators, cognitive scientists, and the people building these tools—and a willingness to measure outcomes that might not align with maximizing engagement.

r001.rationale: The response calls for longitudinal studies with people and comparisons of AI designs, but it does not state that determining which model behaviors to track requires real-world human-subjects research.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to start by asking what we want people to become better at. Is the goal to finish an assignment faster, or is it to understand something well enough that you can explain it, question it, and use it in a different situation? Those are different outcomes, and a system can improve one while undermining another.

So I’d want evaluations that look beyond the interaction itself. After using the system, what can a person do without it? What do they remember a week later? Are they better at judging whether an answer is right, or more inclined to accept whatever sounds confident? And we need to study that over time, because the immediate convenience is much easier to measure than a gradual change in someone’s habits of thought.

We also need to compare different designs. An AI that gives you an answer immediately may have a very different effect from one that asks you to make an attempt, offers a hint, and helps you examine your reasoning. The question isn’t just whether AI helps learning. It’s which kinds of interaction help, for whom, and under what conditions.

That takes independent research, participation from teachers and learners, and companies willing to make their systems available for meaningful scrutiny. Ultimately, success should mean that people gain understanding and agency—not simply that they spend more time with the product.

r001.rationale: The response calls for evaluations after system use, long-term study, and participation from teachers and learners, but it does not state that real-world human-subjects research is required to determine which AI behaviors to track.
